passage: I'm Dolma, and for the clean-lake week I wrote a slogan on chart paper: 'Our lake, our shame, fix it now.' I was proud of it, short and loud. Then my friend Anirban read it and frowned. "Shame? It sounds like you're blaming the whole colony, including the old aunties who've swept that shore for years." I hadn't meant that at all. I meant urgency. I looked at it again and saw that a short line can lean in several directions at once. I tried three more until I found 'Our lake, our care, start today.' My caption for the photo went with it, and it felt warmer. I'm still learning that fewer words means each one carries more.

qa.q: What was Dolma's first slogan?
qa.a: Dolma's first slogan was 'Our lake, our shame, fix it now.'

qa.q: Why did Anirban frown at the word shame?
qa.a: Anirban felt it sounded like blaming the whole colony, including the older neighbours who had cleaned the shore for years. Dolma had meant urgency, so the same words carried a different message for Anirban.

qa.q: What could Dolma try when writing a slogan next time?
qa.a: Show it to a few different people first and ask how each one reads it, then adjust the words.

qa.q: How might one of the aunties who sweep the shore feel about the first slogan?
qa.a: They might feel accused or overlooked, despite their years of work.

grounding: A teen writes a slogan and learns short forms compress attitude and can be read differently by different audiences.

passage: Note, Friday. The Class Nine skit script by Kashish arrived on my desk with the line, 'Everyone in this town is afraid of the truth.' She had also written a caption for the poster: 'Speak up, or stay silent forever.' The words are strong, and I can see she cares about speaking up. But I asked her to imagine how a shy student, or a parent in the audience, might hear them. She was quiet for a bit, then said she hadn't thought of that and wondered if the line sounded like a scolding. She's going to try 'Some of us are afraid of the truth, and that's human.' I will help with the caption too. Avni, drama teacher.

qa.q: What did the poster caption say?
qa.a: The caption said, 'Speak up, or stay silent forever.'

qa.q: What might Kashish have felt when asked how a shy student would hear the line?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised and a bit self-conscious, since she says she hadn't thought of it and wonders if it sounds like scolding. She clearly cares about the message.

qa.q: What could Kashish do with the caption?
qa.a: Try softer, more inclusive wording and test it on a few readers.

qa.q: How might a shy student in the audience feel about the original line?
qa.a: They may feel accused or pressured, instead of invited.

grounding: A teen's script and caption compress attitude, and different audiences read them differently.

passage:
Tuesday
Our class is running the no-plastic campaign, and I got to write the slogan. I spent all of maths on it. Final version: "Bag it, don't bin it!" I was so proud. Short, rhymes, fits on a badge.
Then Irfan read it at break and said, "Wait, bag what? Put the plastic in a bag?"
I said no, bring a cloth bag, don't throw plastic in the bin.
He said, "The little kids will think it means put plastic in a bag and keep it."
I wanted to argue. But then I asked my cousin in Class 3, and she said exactly what Irfan said.
So now it's "Carry cloth, not plastic." Less clever. But the Class 3 kids get it, and they're the ones who throw most of the wrappers.
Five words can mean five things, depending on who's reading.
- Arohi

qa.q: What was Arohi's first slogan?
qa.a: "Bag it, don't bin it!"

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when Irfan questioned the slogan?
qa.a: Arohi felt proud of the slogan and a bit defensive, wanting to argue, before checking and accepting the point.

qa.q: What small step helped Arohi fix the slogan?
qa.a: Testing it on a Class 3 cousin, the actual audience, showed how younger children would read it.

qa.q: How might the Class 3 students read the first slogan?
qa.a: They might take it literally as putting plastic into a bag and keeping it, missing the message about cloth bags.

grounding: The diary shows a teenager writing a campaign slogan whose compressed meaning is read differently by a different audience.

passage:
In the village of Kothur, Ira and Shalini were writing a skit for the Gram Sabha on saving water. Their first script ended with a big line: "Men waste, women carry!"
They practised it at the well. Shalini's uncle heard and frowned. "So all of us are wasters now?" Two other men walked off.
Ira was annoyed. "But it's true in our lane! Who fetches water every morning?"
Shalini thought for a while. "True, but if half the audience walks out, who hears the rest?"
They sat on the well's edge and rewrote it. The new last scene showed a father and a daughter both carrying pots, then fixing a leaking tap together. The last line became: "Every drop, every hand."
At the Gram Sabha, the men clapped. Afterwards Shalini's uncle came up and asked where he could get the tap washers.

qa.q: What was the first script's big line?
qa.a: "Men waste, women carry!"

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when the men walked off?
qa.a: Ira felt annoyed and frustrated, because the line reflected something real in their lane.

qa.q: Which choice of the girls worked, and why?
qa.a: Rewriting the ending to show everyone sharing the work kept the message but let the whole audience hear it without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How did Shalini's uncle read the first line?
qa.a: He read it as an insult to all men, calling them wasters, which made him stop listening.

grounding: The scene shows teenagers writing a skit script whose short line compresses an attitude that different audiences read differently.

passage: The student council at their Addis Ababa school had one day to make posters to save the old vegetable garden, which the principal wanted to pave for parking. Hana stayed up with markers and brought her slogan in huge green letters: GROW IT OR LOSE IT. Her classmates loved it. Abebe punched the air. "That's it. That's us." But at break Mr Tesfaye stopped in front of the poster and frowned. "Is this a threat? Lose what? Your respect for the principal?" Hana's face fell. She had only meant losing the garden. Abebe read it again, slowly, as if he were a teacher. "He's not wrong. It does sound like a warning." They stood there for five minutes, trying words. Finally Hana crossed out the last three and wrote underneath, smaller: GROW IT. SHARE IT. EAT IT. Mr Tesfaye came by later and laughed. "That one I would sign."

qa.q: What did Hana's first slogan say?
qa.a: It said GROW IT OR LOSE IT in huge green letters.

qa.q: What was Hana feeling when Mr Tesfaye asked 'Is this a threat?'
qa.a: Hana felt disappointed and a bit hurt, her face falling, since she only meant losing the garden; she may also have been surprised that four words could be read so differently.

qa.q: How did Hana and Abebe fix the slogan?
qa.a: They reread it the way a teacher might, tried words for five minutes and changed it to GROW IT. SHARE IT. EAT IT., which kept the energy but lost the warning.

qa.q: Why might Mr Tesfaye react differently from Hana's classmates?
qa.a: The classmates heard team spirit, while Mr Tesfaye heard a possible warning to the principal; the same short words fit both readings.

grounding: It shows a teenager's campaign slogan compressing attitude into a few words and being read one way by peers and another way by a teacher.
